summary: Describes the Privacy Pass architecture and the requirements for its protocols, which allow authorization using privacy-preserving authentication. It covers the conceptual model, security and privacy goals, deployment models, and recommendations for each. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a ticket that proves you are allowed in without telling the doorman who you are. This describes how such tickets work and how to use them safely.

questions: how does privacy pass protect privacy
what are privacy pass deployment models
subtitle: Privacy-preserving authentication and authorization with unlinkable tokens.

tldr.problem: Traditional authorization relies on tracking information like cookies that link multiple client interactions, compromising privacy. Services need a way to verify legitimate clients without learning their identity.
tldr.mechanism: Privacy Pass provides a system where clients obtain tokens through privacy-preserving attestation and present these unlinkable tokens for authorization, preventing servers from correlating multiple client interactions.
tldr.outcome: Clients can access services with authorization proof while remaining unidentifiable to servers. The architecture supports multiple deployment models to balance privacy, security, and operational needs.

today: RFC 9576 is an Informational RFC that was published in June 2024. It describes the architecture for Privacy Pass, which is being actively deployed in the web ecosystem for privacy-preserving authorization.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Privacy Pass is an architecture for authorization based on privacy-preserving authentication. Instead of servers learning who a client is, clients present cryptographic proofs that attest to properties about them without revealing their identity.

Traditional authorization mechanisms like cookies allow servers to track clients across sessions and interactions. Privacy Pass takes a different approach: clients present unlinkable tokens that prove they have passed attestation, such as solving a CAPTCHA or proving valid device attestation. Because tokens cannot be linked back to the protocol interaction where they were issued, servers see only that a client is authorized, not which specific client it is.
sections.plainLanguage: Privacy Pass is a way to prove you are allowed to do something without the server knowing who you are. Instead of showing an ID card, you show a ticket that says someone checked you out, without saying who you are.

sections.title: The Four Participants
sections.content:
The Privacy Pass architecture involves four logical entities that interact to issue and redeem tokens.

Client: An entity that seeks authorization to use a resource. Clients run the attestation procedure to prove properties about themselves, such as completing a CAPTCHA.

Origin: A server that wants to authorize clients. Origins challenge clients for tokens and verify them to make authorization decisions.

Attester: An entity that confirms a client meets specific properties required for token issuance. Attesters might verify that a client solved a CAPTCHA, has a valid account, or runs on a trusted device. Attesters trust the client to be legitimate.

Issuer: An entity that generates tokens after a client completes attestation. Issuers create tokens that clients can later present to Origins. Issuers trust Attesters to have correctly verified clients.

These four entities work together: the Client runs attestation with the Attester, the Attester confirms the Client is legitimate, the Issuer creates tokens based on this attestation, and the Client redeems tokens with the Origin.
sections.plainLanguage: Four people work together: you prove you are not a robot to a security checker, the checker tells the ticket office you passed, the ticket office gives you a ticket, and you use the ticket at the door without saying who you are.

sections.title: Token Redemption and Issuance
sections.content:
Privacy Pass involves two main protocols: redemption and issuance.

Redemption: When a client wants access to a resource, the Origin sends a token challenge. If the client has a cached token that matches the challenge, it can present the token immediately. Otherwise, the client must obtain a new token.

Issuance: To obtain a token, the client first runs an attestation procedure with an Attester to prove it meets required properties. Once attestation succeeds, the client sends a token request to the Issuer. The Issuer generates a token response that allows the client to create a token that is cryptographically bound to the token challenge from the Origin. Critically, the Issuer never learns the token challenge itself, ensuring the issuer cannot link the token to later redemptions.

The structure of a token and what properties it might contain depend on the issuance protocol being used. Some tokens support public metadata that clients can observe, while others support private metadata that only the Issuer knows about when creating the token.
sections.plainLanguage: First, you prove to the security checker you are allowed (attestation). Then the ticket office gives you a special blank ticket and a recipe. You use that recipe with your unique challenge to create a filled-out ticket that nobody can trace back to you.

sections.title: Deployment Models
sections.content:
The same four logical entities can be deployed in different ways, creating different trust and privacy properties.

Shared Model: The Origin, Attester, and Issuer are all run by the same entity. This is the simplest model but offers the least privacy because one party sees everything. Tokens must be cached or separated in time from redemption to prevent linkage.

Joint Attester-Issuer: The Attester and Issuer are operated together by a trusted third party, separate from the Origin. This allows the Origin to offload attestation and issuance while maintaining some privacy separation between attestation and redemption contexts.

Joint Origin-Issuer: The Origin and Issuer are run by the same entity, separate from the Attester. This is useful when Origins need client-identifying attestation like account verification, but do not want to learn client IP addresses beyond what appears during token redemption.

Split Model: The Origin, Attester, and Issuer are all operated by different entities. This is the most general model where each entity only sees information necessary for its role. The Attester sees client-identifying information, the Issuer sees issuance details, and the Origin sees only tokens and challenges.

Each model involves different assumptions about which entities will or will not collude, and correspondingly different implications for client privacy and anonymity set size.
sections.plainLanguage: These four roles can be split among one, two, or more companies depending on what privacy is needed. If they all work for the same company, they share everything. If they are separate, each sees only what they need.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Goals
sections.content:
Privacy Pass aims to achieve four unlinkability properties that form its core privacy goals.

Origin-Client unlinkability: An Origin cannot determine whether two token redemptions come from the same client or different clients. All clients in a redemption context appear indistinguishable to the Origin.

Issuer-Client unlinkability: An Issuer cannot link clients across different token issuance events, even if it sees multiple issuance requests.

Attester-Origin unlinkability: An Attester cannot determine whether two attestation contexts correspond to the same Origin or different Origins, preventing the Attester from learning which service a client is trying to access.

Redemption context unlinkability: An Origin cannot determine which attestation or issuance events correspond to a specific token redemption, even if the Issuer and Attester share information.

These unlinkability properties ensure that clients can correlate information about themselves across interactions, but the Attester, Issuer, and Origin cannot link information across their respective functions.

Privacy can be compromised through several channels: IP addresses, metadata attached to tokens, key rotation that partitions clients into different anonymity sets, and side-channel timing attacks that reveal which clients started issuance at similar times.
sections.plainLanguage: Privacy Pass wants to make sure that: the ticket office cannot recognize you later, the security checker does not learn which service you are accessing, and the doorman cannot tell which ticket office you visited. It works best when no one learns your IP address along the way.
